trial_name: TELESCOPE — Effect of Tele-ICU on Clinical Outcomes of Critically Ill Patients (2024)
citation: Pereira AJ, Noritomi DT, dos Santos MC, et al; TELESCOPE Trial Investigators. Effect of Tele-ICU on Clinical Outcomes of Critically Ill Patients: The TELESCOPE Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2024;332(21):1798-1807
one_liner: A pragmatic cluster-randomized trial of weekday tele-ICU rounds in Brazilian public ICUs did not reduce ICU length of stay or hospital mortality.

pico.population: Adult general ICUs in Brazilian public hospitals without structured daily intensivist-led multidisciplinary rounds or regular audit/feedback; patients ≥18 years
pico.intervention: Daily (Mon–Fri) tele-ICU multidisciplinary rounds with remote intensivist, ICU nurse, RT; monthly audit/feedback meetings; dissemination of 19 clinical protocols and e-learning
pico.comparison: Usual bedside care without tele-ICU rounds, audit/feedback, or protocol package
pico.outcome: Primary: ICU length of stay (first ICU admission). Secondary: hospital mortality, CLABSI, VAE, ventilator-free days, feeding, sedation, oxygenation, ICU-level SMR/SRU

background.existing_knowledge: Tele-ICU is promoted to extend intensivist expertise to ICUs with limited on-site specialists, but prior evidence is mostly observational and heterogeneous, with models ranging from continuous monitoring to advisory rounds.
background.knowledge_gap: The causal effect of a tele-ICU program based on daily multidisciplinary rounds, audit/feedback, and protocol dissemination on patient outcomes in resource-constrained public ICUs is unknown.
background.hypothesis: The intervention would reduce ICU length of stay by improving care processes and facilitating earlier ICU discharge.

methods.design: Pragmatic, multicenter, parallel-group, cluster-randomised clinical trial (ICU as unit of randomisation) with 30 ICUs, batched randomisation (5 blocks), 2-month baseline, 1-month transition, 13-month intervention period.
methods.setting: 30 adult general (mixed medical–surgical) ICUs in public hospitals across all Brazilian regions; on-site physicians and nurses; ≥8 ICU beds.

inclusion: Adults ≥18 years admitted to participating ICUs during the trial periods.
exclusion: admissions during the waiting/transition period between randomisation and evaluation start.

methods.intervention: Daily (Mon–Fri) tele-ICU multidisciplinary rounds led by remote board-certified intensivist with ICU nurse and RT, using a structured daily care plan, conducted with the local ICU team via a mobile rack with PC, microphone, and 4K 360° camera. Monthly virtual meetings to discuss ICU performance indicators with local leadership. Dissemination of 19 evidence-based clinical protocols and e-learning materials (text/video).
methods.comparison: Usual bedside ICU care without tele-rounds, audit/feedback, or protocol e-learning package. COVID-19 protocols and training videos shared with both groups after pandemic onset to mitigate bias.
methods.blinding: Unblinded (cluster-level service delivery); objective outcomes reduce detection bias risk.
methods.sample_size_power: 15,000 patients to detect a 1.5-day absolute reduction in ICU LOS (baseline mean 8 days, SD 10) with 80% power, 2-sided α 0.05, ICC 0.018, variable cluster sizes.
methods.primary_outcome: ICU length of stay (days) for first ICU admission.
secondary_outcomes: Incidence of central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) per 1,000 CVC-days
Incidence of ventilator-associated events (VAE) per 1,000 ventilator-days
Receiving enteral or parenteral feeding per 100 patient-days
Light sedation or alert/calm per 100 ventilator-days
methods.follow_up: From ICU admission until ICU discharge or death; truncated at 90 days in hospital from ICU admission.

headline_bullets: Primary outcome (ICU LOS) not reduced: 8.1 vs 7.1 days, adjusted % change +8.2% (95% CI −5.4% to 23.8%; p=0.24).
Moderate implementation fidelity: tele-visits on 68% of eligible patient-days, 74% recommendation acceptance, 62% monthly meetings completed.

outcomes_table.outcome: Primary: ICU length of stay (days), first ICU admission
outcomes_table.note: Adjusted median difference 0 days (95% CI −2 to 3)

outcomes_table.outcome: Incidence of ventilator-associated events per 1,000 ventilator-days

safety: Ventilator-associated events: 16.3 vs 17.1 per 1000 vent-days (IRR 1.02; 95% CI 0.82–1.27).

domains.notes: Cluster randomisation with batched blocks, restricted algorithm to minimise baseline imbalance. Allocation concealment not feasible at cluster level.
Unblinded service-delivery intervention. Objective outcomes (LOS, mortality) reduce detection bias, but co-intervention risk remains.
No cluster dropouts. Primary analysis ITT on first ICU admission; readmissions excluded. Patients during waiting/transition period excluded by design.
Tele-visits on 68% of eligible patient-days (median 72%), 151,723 recommendations with 74% acceptance, monthly meetings completed 62%. COVID-19 protocols shared with both arms, reducing separation.
Groups broadly comparable in age, SAPS3, SOFA; some difference in mechanical ventilation at admission (48.7% vs 42.2%). Analyses adjusted for prognostic covariates.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate: strong pragmatic design, large sample, objective outcomes, and pre-published protocol support causal inference. Unblinded delivery, variable fidelity, and pandemic-era co-interventions plausibly limited detectable effects.

domains.notes: Adult general ICUs in Brazilian public hospitals without structured intensivist-led rounds; matches resource-constrained, public-sector ICUs but not high-intensity academic ICUs.

Evaluated an advisory rounds-based tele-ICU model with weekday coverage. Findings apply to similar programmes, not to continuous monitoring or direct-authority tele-ICU models. Sensitivity to discharge pathways and bed availability may limit generalisability.

external_validity.verdict: Good generalisability to under-resourced public ICUs considering advisory rounds-based tele-ICU; limited for high-intensity ICUs or continuous monitoring models.

strengths: Large, pragmatic cluster-randomised evaluation at scale (30 ICUs; 15,230 patients).
Clinically and policy-relevant setting (public Brazilian ICUs).
Objective primary and key secondary outcomes.
Detailed implementation metrics (tele-round coverage, recommendation volume/acceptance).
Published protocol and statistical analysis plan supporting transparency.
limitations: Unblinded service-delivery intervention introduces risk of performance bias and co-intervention.
Heterogeneous context across ICUs and substantial COVID-19 pandemic overlap (73.5% of patients enrolled post-pandemic onset), with shared protocols potentially diluting between-group differences.
Moderate intervention intensity: tele-visits on only 68% of eligible patient-days; monthly meetings completed 62%.
Primary outcome (ICU LOS) is system-sensitive and may be less responsive to clinical decision support in strained public systems.
Some secondary outcomes reported without p-values; interpretation relies on confidence intervals.

critical_appraisal.summary: A well-designed cluster RCT with objective endpoints, but negative results may partly reflect modest implementation fidelity and pandemic-era contamination, limiting confidence in concluding that tele-ICU rounds have no benefit.
weaknesses: Primary outcome influenced by system factors

sections.authors_conclusion: In this pragmatic public-ICU setting, a weekday tele-rounds-based tele-ICU programme did not shorten ICU length of stay or reduce hospital mortality, arguing against assuming that tele-rounds alone, even with frequent recommendations, necessarily improve outcomes.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial does not support routine implementation of weekday tele-ICU rounds with audit/feedback for improving patient outcomes in similar public ICUs.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Public general ICUs lacking structured intensivist-led rounds, especially in resource-limited settings.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That tele-ICU is uniformly ineffective; this specific advisory model with moderate fidelity failed to improve outcomes.
implementation_caveats: Tele-ICU effectiveness likely depends on model (advisory vs. continuous monitoring), fidelity, and local system constraints.
Higher-intensity models (e.g., continuous monitoring with decision authority) may yield different results.

controversies.notes: Tele-ICU encompasses diverse models (advisory rounds, continuous monitoring, decision authority); prior evidence is inconsistent. The negative TELESCOPE result may not apply to other models.
ICU LOS is objective but shaped by organisational factors (step-down capacity, bed strain); improved clinical processes may not translate into shorter LOS, potentially biasing toward null.

Moderate tele-round coverage (68% of eligible days) and incomplete monthly meetings (62%) raise the possibility that the tested 'real-world dose' was insufficient to move outcomes, despite 151,723 recommendations (74% accepted).

controversies.topic: Need for rigorous evaluation of complex technology
controversies.notes: Editorial commentary emphasised that tele-ICU requires careful attention to context and implementation; TELESCOPE exemplifies a rigorous yet negative pragmatic trial.

Meta-analyses suggesting tele-ICU benefit are limited by heterogeneity and predominantly non-randomised studies; TELESCOPE adds large randomised evidence of no clear benefit for advisory rounds-based models.

unresolved_questions: Would a more intensive tele-ICU model (continuous monitoring, decision authority) improve patient-centred outcomes?
What is the optimal implementation strategy to achieve higher fidelity in similar settings?
How did the COVID-19 pandemic context influence these results, and would effects differ in a non-pandemic era?
Would outcomes improve with a more robust discharge facilitation component or with higher-acuity ICUs?

numbers_to_remember: ICU LOS: 8.1 vs 7.1 days, adjusted % change +8.2% (95% CI −5.4% to 23.8%), p=0.24
Tele-visits on 68% of eligible patient-days; 151,723 recommendations with 74% acceptance
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Weekday tele-ICU rounds in Brazilian public ICUs did not shorten ICU stay or reduce mortality, highlighting that tele-ICU benefit is not guaranteed without high fidelity and consideration of local system constraints.
